intro.heading: The policy nobody thought to write.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: A registered manager takes over a service and inherits a tidy shelf of folders. Safeguarding, medication, infection control and complaints are all there, and each has a review date. Nobody has ever asked a different question, which is what is not on the shelf. Over the years a service adds a hydration plan here and a new type of equipment there, and the policy set stays as it was. The manager is confident because every folder looks in order. Then a deputy mentions that nothing explains how the home deals with legionella. Here is how that plays out.

trail.text: A new manager takes over a service and inherits a full shelf of policies.
Each folder has a cover sheet and a review date.
The core subjects are all there. The manager relaxes.
Nobody has asked what the set does not cover.
Policies were added when something went wrong, never from a list.
A folder called Health and Safety may say nothing about water.
A shelf that looks complete and no way to prove it is.
“Where is your policy on this?” The folder is not there.

trail_close: The shelf was never the problem. The gap is between what a library looks like and what its content covers. Here is how CareStream reads your own policies and tells you what the evidence says is missing.

items.q: Will CareStream give me a list of every policy my home needs?
items.a: No, and we would be wary of any tool that claimed to. It looks at what your own policies say and checks that against a set of regulations matched to your type of service. Where nothing in your library covers a regulation, it suggests a policy to add. It works from evidence in your policies, not from a fixed list.

items.q: How does it decide a policy is missing?
items.a: It reads the content of your policies, not their titles. For each regulation it asks whether any policy is actually about that subject, and then whether that policy contains what it should. Only a subject with no policy behind it counts as missing. So a mislabelled folder cannot fool it either way.

items.q: Is it a verdict I have to act on?
items.a: No. It is a suggestion. You can ignore it, restore it later, or add a written policy. It also stays quiet if the result looks out of date, for example when policies have changed since the last run.

items.q: What happens when I want the missing policy?
items.a: You can buy a written policy from the CareStream policy shop. It is written from your service details, checked by a gate, then read by a person before it arrives in your library. It goes through your own approval steps like any other policy, and the next coverage run reads it as evidence. The shop is separate from the subscription.

items.q: Do I need to turn the new policy into training?
items.a: It helps. Once the policy is in, you can allocate a short training module built from your own policies. Staff do it in the Staff Hub, and a wrong answer goes to their Follow-up tab, where they choose Learn & retry or Just retry. You see the result in the Knowledge gaps view, and a Monday digest arrives by email.

items.q: Does CareStream rewrite my policies for me?
items.a: Not on its own. It suggests wording, and an admin adopts or ignores each suggestion. Adopted wording becomes a tracked change in a draft, and nothing reaches staff until it passes your approval steps. The example wording is drafted by our own machine learning, so read it as a starting point.

items.q: Can I try this without paying?
items.a: There is a free route that checks up to 5 uploaded policies in total, with all four analyses, and paid plans have a 14 day free trial. Gap detection and fixes are Professional and above. Create a free account to see it on your own policies.

items.q: Will this get me a good CQC rating?
items.a: No. It gives you a clearer picture and a record of what you did about it. The wording it suggests is guidance, not legal advice, and you decide what your service adopts.

faqs.heading: Care home policies and procedures, answered

items.q: What care home policies and procedures does a service need?
items.a: There is no single national list. What you need depends on your type of service and the regulated activities you carry out. A check against the regulations that apply to you is a safer starting point than a generic list. Our guide to policies required by CQC explains how to approach it.

The Care Quality Commission does not publish a set of policies for you to copy. It inspects whether your service has the governance and the records it needs. Its guidance on Regulation 17 lists governance arrangements such as policies and procedures among those records.

items.q: Is a policy template enough for a care home?
items.a: A policy template is a starting point, not a finished policy. It may not reflect your service, and templates from different places can contradict each other. Read our post on why downloaded templates create contradictions.

items.q: How do I find out which care policies I am missing?
items.a: Read what your policies actually say against the regulations that apply to you. CareStream does this with a coverage check, and a regulation with no policy behind it is suggested as a missing policy.

items.q: How often should a policy review happen?
items.a: There is no fixed legal interval, so set one that suits each policy and keep to it. The CQC says systems and processes should be continually reviewed to make sure they remain fit for purpose. See how often care policies should be reviewed.

items.q: Does the missing policy check cost tokens?
items.a: Showing the missing policies is read only and free. It relies on a coverage run, which uses tokens, so run that first. The separate out of date scan uses none.

items.q: Is the missing policy check on every plan?
items.a: The free route checks up to 5 uploaded policies in total. Gap detection and the fixes are on Professional and above. See pricing for the current plans.

items.q: Do I have to buy the policy from CareStream?
items.a: No. You can write your own, use one from elsewhere, or ignore the suggestion. Whatever you add, upload it, and the next coverage run reads it as evidence.

items.q: Does it replace my own policy review?
items.a: No. It supports it. A person still decides what the policy should say, and the guide below shows a simple way to run a review.

guide.heading: A practical way to check your policy set
guide.lede: Care home policies and procedures only protect people if they cover the right subjects, and a regular review is how you find out. Under the regulations, systems and processes must be established and operated effectively, so a review of what you have is part of good governance.

sections.h3: Start with what each policy actually says
paragraphs: Do not trust titles. Open each policy and ask what subject it truly covers, who owns it and when it was last reviewed. A policy named Health and Safety may not cover water, and a policy called Safeguarding may be silent on what staff do after a disclosure. A short list of subjects against folders will show where you have no cover at all.

sections.h3: A simple policy review for a busy service
checklist: List every subject your service deals with, including equipment and specialist care.
Match each subject to the policy that really covers it, by content and not by title.
Mark anything with no match as a gap, and decide whether to write, buy or ignore it.
Set a review date and a named owner for every policy, then tell staff what changed.

guide.note: For the inspector. Keep the date of each check, what you found and what you decided, so you can show a policy set that is reviewed and not only filed.
